title: From India to Gaza: Youth Revolts and the Struggle to Break Open the Future
author: Henry Giroux
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Dinkan_poster_in_NEET_paper_leak_protest_bengaluru-680x510.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/31/from-
india-to-gaza-youth-revolts-and-the-struggle-to-break-open-the-future/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Dinkan_poster_in_NEET_paper_leak_protest_bengaluru-680x510.jpg)

Photograph Source: Subin Siby -
[CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en)

> “What if all the cockroaches come together?”
>
> – [Abhijeet Dipke](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cz72y11jjq1o)

Marx and Engels issued the historic call: “Workers of the world, unite! You
have nothing to lose but your chains!” Today, that summons returns with
renewed urgency and takes a new form: Young people of the world unite and
resist. Youth today possess the courage, imagination, anger, and numbers to
change the course of history. They have grown up in societies paralyzed by
cynicism, loneliness, desperation, and hatred, conditions that isolate people
from one another and teach them to regard cruelty as inevitable. Yet even amid
this desolation, a radical possibility remains: the recovery of solidarity as
a passion for justice and love as a public and collective force. This militant
love begins with the recognition that our lives are profoundly interconnected,
that freedom cannot be reduced to individual escape, and that none of us can
be secure while others are rendered vulnerable and disposable. It creates
bonds strong enough to break through isolation, connect private suffering to
public responsibility, and transform compassion into organized resistance**.**
As James Baldwin and Malcolm X understood in different ways, learning to live
requires learning to love, not as sentimentality or a retreat into private
life, but as a refusal of hatred, racism, and the machinery of disposability.

Militant love takes the side of justice. It finds expression in solidarity,
shared struggle, and the willingness to assume responsibility for lives beyond
our immediate experience. It transforms loneliness into connection, despair
into collective courage, and anger into a disciplined struggle for a world in
which no human being is considered expendable. With catastrophe no longer on
the horizon but at their doorstep, young people must build a worldwide
movement of resistance that neither propaganda nor repression can silence. It
is time to bring to a halt the machinery of death sustained by governments and
their military-industrial-academic institutions, all stained by the suffering
of children, women, the elderly, and those condemned as disposable.

But solidarity becomes a radical force only when moral conviction takes the
form of organized struggle. Student-led protests in India have demonstrated
how culture can become both a pedagogical weapon and a vehicle of collective
resistance. After Chief Justice of India Surya Kant contemptuously referred to
unemployed young people as “cockroaches,” [**Abhijeet
Dipke**](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cz72y11jjq1o)**** answered with a
provocative challenge on Instagram: “What if all cockroaches come together?”
The question spread rapidly, transforming an insult meant to humiliate into a
rallying cry of defiance. Confronting the corrupt and increasingly
authoritarian Modi government, students, unemployed young people, and their
supporters used memes, satire, and Instagram reels to expose corruption,
puncture the mythology of power, and mobilize mass protest. [Met with tear
gas, police violence, and detention, they refused to abandon the
streets.](https://jacobin.com/2026/07/india-student-protest-state-violence)
Their resistance revealed that domination is sustained through more than
force. It also depends on images, narratives, and a manufactured common sense
that teaches people what to fear, accept, and obey. [By turning culture
against power,](https://countercurrents.org/2026/07/when-a-nation-found-its-
voice-how-gen-z-reawakened-indian-democracy/) the protesters entered the very
terrain where identities are formed, anger finds a language, and private
suffering becomes public outrage and collective action.

[The youth-led Cockroach Janta
Party](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/20/who-are-indias-cockroach-
janta-party-and-why-are-they-staging-protests-) converted this defiance into a
rapidly expanding movement. [With more than 20 million followers on Instagram,
it built an alternative public sphere beyond the government’s propaganda
machine.](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/29/gen-z-movement-triumphs-in-
the-land-of-gandhi/)Young people turned digital ridicule into political
solidarity and carried it from the screen into the streets. Images of police
repression widened public outrage, while the movement’s growing power [forced
the resignation of India’s education
minister](https://countercurrents.org/2026/07/massive-student-protests-which-
forced-dharmendra-pradhan-to-resign-a-sign-of-downfall-for-the-bjp/) and
placed educational reform and public accountability on the national agenda.
[As Arundhati Roy notes](https://www.equator.org/articles/cockroach-janata-
party-arundhati-
roy?utm_source=brevo&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Equator+newsletter+38+-+250726+FREE),
“the student protesters who have swarmed Delhi are showing us a different
future for India.”

[What began as an insult became a
symbol](https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-interactive/2026/jul/25/i-will-
die-for-this-cause-how-indias-cockroach-meme-became-the-biggest-challenge-to-
modis-grip-on-power). What began as a meme became a movement. What began
online became a material force capable of making an authoritarian government
retreat. This was more than a new style of protest. [It was a restructuring of
politics from below](https://countercurrents.org/2026/07/indias-youth-write-a-
historic-chapter-in-democratic-resistance/), one that seized the cultural
technologies of domination and turned them against the systems of power that
produce censorship and dispossession. It showed that culture is not an
ornament to politics; it is one of the decisive sites where power is
challenged, solidarity is created, and collective agency is born.

The lesson extends far beyond India. It must not be lost on young people in
the United States or elsewhere, especially as the genocidal assault on Gaza is
accompanied by an accelerating campaign of state and settler violence in the
occupied West Bank. The catastrophe in Palestine is not confined to Gaza. [It
is part of a broader colonial
projec](https://yellowheadinstitute.org/2026/the-palestine-example-the-
problem-of-gaza-genocide-exceptionalism/)t of dispossession, forced
displacement, territorial theft, and the destruction of Palestinian life, a
logic of domination increasingly visible across the globe. It is also a
warning of what awaits the rest of the world as emerging fascist states answer
economic crisis with racist paranoia, militarism, and fantasies of
purification. This violence involves more than the crushing of dissent. A
gangster form of neoliberal capitalism is merging with colonial violence and
authoritarian rule, producing a criminogenic order in which law serves power,
cruelty becomes policy, and entire populations are abandoned to injury, exile,
and death. Azeezah Kanji is right to insist:

We speak often of the “Palestine exception”: the extreme repression of
Palestinian and Palestine solidarity speech and activism. We ought also to
speak of the Palestine example: understanding Palestine not simply as an
exception, but as an emblem of the colonial modern condition.

[The assault on the village of Tell](https://www.savageminds.co/p/the-spark-
in-tell?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffb08273c-3eca-4a22-8a11-09e39ce98002_1440x810.jpeg&open=false),
southwest of Nablus, gives concrete meaning to this “Palestine example”:
colonial power operating through the combined forces of the military, the
state, and armed settlers to dispossess a people and destroy the conditions
necessary for collective life**.** Following a deadly confrontation involving
Palestinians, armed settlers, and Israeli forces, the Israeli government
imposed collective punishment. Four Palestinians were killed, dozens were
detained, homes were raided, and military operations spread across neighboring
communities. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a wider military
campaign, while members of his far-right government demanded further
settlement expansion and the depopulation of Palestinian villages. [UN Special
Rapporteur Francesca Albanese described the combined army-settler attacks as
pogroms against defenseless civilians. ](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-
east/un-rapporteur-calls-israeli-attacks-in-occupied-west-bank-civilians-
pogroms-/4008948)

Tell is not an isolated incident. [Since October 2023, Israeli forces and
settlers have killed more than 1,000 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank,
including roughly 200 children.](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-
palestinian-territory/un-human-rights-occupied-palestinian-
territory-1001-palestinians-killed-west-bank-7-october-2023-one-five-are-
children-enar) Thousands have been injured, and more than 10,000 have been
displaced by military operations, demolitions, settler attacks, and
restrictions on access to their land. Entire Bedouin and rural communities
have been driven from their homes, while settlement construction and the
seizure of Palestinian territory have proceeded at an unprecedented pace. The
violence of armed settler mobs cannot be separated from the government that
protects, arms, and politically enables them. Nor can it be separated from
[Israel’s widening military assaults across the region, including
Lebanon](https://www.euronews.com/2026/05/27/israel-expands-military-ground-
operations-in-southern-lebanon-as-clashes-with-hezbollah-in). These are not
disconnected eruptions of violence but expressions of a larger politics of
colonial expansion, collective punishment, and permanent war.

[What is unfolding across Gaza and the West Bank is a crime against humanity
made possible by weapons, diplomatic protection, media indifference, and the
shameful complicity of powerful Western
governments,](https://www.palestinechronicle.com/gaza-the-deafening-sound-of-
silence-in-western-political-and-media-circles/) especially the United States.
Universities invest in and collaborate with the institutions that sustain the
war machine. Corporate media turn mass suffering into background noise.
Political leaders empty the language of human rights of all meaning by
applying it selectively. Under these conditions, silence is not neutrality. It
is a form of collaboration, and [the normalization of genocide becomes a
rehearsal for further
crimes](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/21/opinion/israel-gaza-palestinians-
genocide.html).

The young people of India have shown what becomes possible [when a generation
refuses the future imposed upon it.](https://www.laprogressive.com/foreign-
policy/cockroach-janta-party)They are not alone. The resistance emerging among
young people across the world offers a language for confronting this global
regime of violence[. Although sparked by specific grievances, these revolts
are rooted in widening inequality, unemployment, economic insecurity,
corruption, censorship, and the shameless nepotism of political
elites](https://countercurrents.org/2026/07/beyond-intelligence-failure-the-
power-of-a-peoples-uprising/).

What is often missed in the mainstream press is that young protesters are
revolting against a global form of gangster capitalism that has denied them a
meaningful place in the present and robbed them of a future. Commenting on the
Cockroach uprising, [Vijay Prashad](https://www.laprogressive.com/foreign-
policy/cockroach-janta-party) identifies the deeper economic forces driving
this revolt:

The young protesters are not in revolt because they possess shorter attention
spans or a special cultural aversion to authority. They are in revolt because
[capitalism](https://laprogressive.com/election-and-campaigns/political-terms-
used-in-the-united-states#Capitalism) cannot integrate them into dignified
economic life. They have been told to study, acquire degrees, learn new
skills, remain competitive, and become ‘entrepreneurs.’ Their families have
borrowed money, sold land, postponed medical treatment, and reduced household
consumption to pay for education and coaching. At the end of this punishing
journey, many discover that the promised job does not exist. Others find only
temporary contracts, unpaid internships, platform work, or jobs whose wages
bear no relation to their qualifications.

This crisis is not confined to India. [In Bangladesh, student protests brought
an end to Sheikh Hasina’s fifteen-year
rule](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c9033zpv0nvo). [In
Nepal,](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/sep/09/nepal-protests-social-
media-ban-lifted-gen-z-kathmandu) resistance to corruption and digital
censorship forced the prime minister’s resignation. [In
Madagascar,](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/oct/17/gen-z-victory-
young-protesters-toppled-madagascar-leader)protests that began over water and
power cuts grew into demands for “a complete overhaul of the political system”
and drove President Andry Rajoelina from the country. [In
Kenya](https://www.opendemocracy.net/kenyas-gen-z-beat-the-tax-bill-now-were-
coming-for-the-ballot-box/), a decentralized youth movement compelled the
government to withdraw a punishing finance bill and continues to challenge
state power and shape the country’s politics.

Largely leaderless and digitally connected, these movements have transformed
social media into a counter-public sphere and translated online networks into
political power in the streets. Different in their histories, demands, and
results, they share a crucial lesson: when young people refuse silence,
organize across differences, and connect their courage to a broader public
outrage, governments can be forced to retreat and seemingly immovable
structures of power can begin to crack.

The challenge now is to turn these scattered revolts into a common struggle.
Young people everywhere must transform these lessons into an international
movement capable of bringing millions into the streets and interrupting the
institutions that make mass violence possible. They must organize peaceful
demonstrations across borders, build student-worker alliances, occupy public
spaces, radicalize the social imagination, and expose the systems of
propaganda that sustain it. They must demand an immediate end to the
slaughter, an arms embargo, international sanctions, and freedom and justice
for the Palestinian people. Moral outrage must become organized power.

Such a movement must be joined by educators, artists, cultural workers, trade
unionists, journalists, faith communities, and public intellectuals.
Resistance cannot remain fragmented by national borders or confined to
isolated campuses and cities. Demonstrations must become global, coordinated,
sustained, and impossible for governments to ignore. Boycotts, divestment
campaigns, labor actions, teach-ins, and mass civil disobedience must converge
into a broad democratic front capable of imposing a political cost on
complicity. The capitalist and reactionary nationalist institutions that
sustain oppression must be confronted wherever they operate: in government
ministries, corporations, universities, media systems, financial networks, and
the arms industry.

[The Indian youth movement thus offers a lesson that is both cultural and
political. ](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/7/23/televising-our-
revolution-indias-gen-z-flips-modis-social-media-game) Images, algorithms,
digital platforms, and political spectacles are expressions of power, but they
can also be seized as instruments of resistance. Cultural critique must move
beyond exposing how consent is manufactured and desire is organized. The
cultural realm can be reclaimed from below and transformed into a public
pedagogy of resistance, collective courage, and radical democratic
possibility. But digital resistance reaches its limit unless it enters the
streets, builds durable organizations, joins workers and communities, and
converts visibility into lasting political power.

The power of young people lies not in youth alone, but in their capacity to
awaken the rest of society from the paralysis of cynicism, fear, and
manufactured helplessness. They can expose the lie that nothing can change,
connect struggles that power works to keep apart, and give global solidarity
an organized and material form. Yet youthful rebellion cannot be sustained by
the rush of collective energy and the explosive reach of digital culture
alone. As [Vijay Prashad](https://www.laprogressive.com/foreign-
policy/cockroach-janta-party) rightly warns, “spontaneity and digital reach
alone cannot overcome entrenched power.” If the Cockroach movement is to
become a lasting political force, it must link examination reform to what
Prashad calls “broader struggles for employment, public education, labour
rights, and economic redistribution.” The question, then, is no longer whether
young people possess the power to ignite change, but whether people across
generations will join them in building a movement capable of sustaining it.

The burden of resistance does not rest solely with the young. Their movements
provide a map, not an alibi for the inaction of others. They have revealed the
language, imagination, courage, and forms of struggle required of everyone who
refuses a future organized around genocide, colonialism, and permanent war.
Gaza is being destroyed. The West Bank is being emptied village by village.
The politics of genocidal violence is spreading across the globe. The time for
isolated gestures and ceremonial outrage has passed. What is needed now is a
worldwide uprising of conscience transformed into disciplined, sustained,
nonviolent mass resistance. Young people of the world must unite with workers,
educators, artists, and all those who refuse a world ruled by cruelty,
dispossession, and war. They must organize to shut down the institutions that
feed the war machine, making complicity impossible and solidarity unavoidable.
At stake is whether the future will belong to the merchants of death or to
those with the courage to stop them. Neutrality is no longer an option.
Resistance is an imperative.
